theory_title: Losses hurt about twice as much as gains please
theory_content: Losing ₹10,000 feels roughly twice as bad as gaining ₹10,000 feels good. This asymmetry explains why people hold losing positions hoping to break even, sell winners too early to lock in a feeling, and keep money in savings accounts during decades when equity outperformed. Knowing the bias does not remove it; building rules in advance is what does.

The price you paid becomes the reference point for every later decision, even though the market has no idea what you paid. "I will sell when it gets back to ₹500" is anchoring. The only question that carries information is whether you would buy it today at today’s price.

theory_title: The last twelve months feel like the future
theory_content: After a strong year, investors raise their expectations and their allocation; after a crash, they cut both. This is precisely backwards, and it is most of the 1.7% annual gap between what funds return and what their investors earn. Written rules, applied on a schedule, are the standard defence.

theory_title: Research that was never going to change your mind
theory_content: Once you own something, you read about it differently: supporting views feel rigorous, contrary ones feel uninformed. The practical counter is to write down, before buying, what would make you sell — a specific number or event. If nothing would, you are not investing, you are supporting.
